newsitem.title: GREECE: Athens bourse has lowest P/E, top div yield - IFC.
newsitem.headline: Athens bourse has lowest P/E, top div yield - IFC.

text.p: Greece's equities market has the lowest price earnings ratio (P/E) -- 14.49 -- and the highest dividend yield -- 4.47 percent -- among European emerging stock markets despite its recent two-month rally, the International Finance Corporation (IFC) said.

"Based on the IFC Investable index, the Greek stock market had the lowest P/E ratio, 14.49, in end February," IFC head market analyst Costantinos Grigoriadis told a business conference on the Balkans in Thessaloniki.
"The market's rally since the beginning of the year has not removed the Athens bourse from first place. It remains the market with the lowest P/E ratio among European emerging markets," he said.
Based on the IFC's investable indices, Istanbul is the best performing bourse in dollar terms so far this year, up 35.1 percent, followed by Athens with 27.1 percent.
The Greek stock market's price-to-book value (P/BV) ratio in end-February was 2.79, below Turkey's 6.6, he said.
Most of Europe's emerging stock markets had managed double digit returns so far this year, reflecting the prevailing strong investment interest for the region's liquid markets.

Europe's southeastern emerging markets had attractive trading multiples compared to other bourses the IFC covers. For example, Athens and Istanbul compared favourably to Argentina which had a P/E of 39.5 in end-February and China with 33.6.
Their low correlation with other emerging stock markets was a significant reason why fund managers investing in these markets needed to include them in their portfolios.

"Greece and Turkey, the Balkan region's two largest stock markets share common characteristics. Both are influenced by politics and social unrest while large foreign capital inflows tend to significantly affect the local share index," he said.
Only three out of the nine Balkan exchanges had average daily trading volume above $1.0 million.
"In end-January, Turkey's stock market traded a daily $283 million on average followed by Greece with $49 million. These two markets virtually monopolise foreign investors' interest," he said.

But aside from its differences with other emerging markets in Latin America and southeast Asia, southeastern Europe shared similarities including low labour costs, high demand for consumer goods and a need for investment in infrastructure.
"Taiwan's stock exchange has 1.5 times more listings but its market capitalisation is 19 times larger than that of the Athens bourse," Grigoriadis told the conference on cooperation in the Balkans.

Attractive valuations, slow but steady privatisation trends, faster GDP growth rates along with a competitive regulatory environment and growing foreign investor interest were the reasons why funds should be invested in southeastern Europe's emerging markets.
According to the World Bank's definition, a market is considered to be emerging when 1995 per capita GDP falls below $9,385.

"In many cases the IFC indices cover markets in countries whose GDP is above the threshold but these remain in the emerging category because their capital markets are growing and also because they are considered emerging markets by the large institutional investors" he said. --George Georgiopoulos, Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
